newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greece stalls talks on future Cyprus EU entry.
newsitem.headline: Greece stalls talks on future Cyprus EU entry.

text.p: A stand-off between Greece and its European Union partners over Cyprus was to push talks on the divided island's EU membership off the agenda of a joint meeting of foreign ministers on Tuesday.

Although EU foreign ministers were to go ahead with an annual association council meeting with Cyprus to review current relations, the most crucial issue of the future was taboo for want of a joint EU position.

In a sign of mounting tension over the island between Turkey and Greece, Athens stonewalled a move by its EU partners on Monday to involve the northern Turkish third of Cyprus in the process of admitting the island to the bloc.
The EU's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek -- who visits Cyprus from Wednesday to meet both communities -- told Reuters Greece's EU partners had not radically shifted position.

"There's a sense of urgency in the EU that we must find a political solution to Cyprus...We want to give a signal to the northern part that the Turkish community should be involved as soon as possible in the accession process," he told Reuters.
"The Greek side felt that this could be seen as a change of position. It was not intended to be," he said.

The EU has vowed to open talks on Cypriot membership at the latest six months after the close of its current inter- governmental review of its workings to prepare the bloc for the day it has up to 25 members.
As part of that process the EU holds regular "structured dialogues" with 11 applicants, and it was that part of Tuesday's meeting which was not to take place.
In 1995, after failing to find a political solution for the island, the EU agreed that Cypriot membership could be limited to its southern Greek part.

Diplomats said on Monday that the move by Greece's 14 EU partners to involve the Turkish part was designed to pressure Athens to negotiate a settlement for the divided island, of which Turkey invaded the northern third in 1974, in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia that was backed by Athens.
The international community, with the exception of Turkey, recognises the Greek Cypriot adminstration as the island's only government.

To complicate matters further Turkey -- whose own request for EU membership has been shunned on human rights grounds -- is threatening to bloc expansion of the NATO military alliance to eastern Europe if the EU continues to keep it at arms leangth.

During his three-day visit to Cyprus van den Broek will meet representatives from both sides of the island, including Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and leader of the Turkish Cypriot community Rauf Denktash.
The Commission said in a statement the talks would concentrate on the future membership plans and the U.N. brokered talks to seek a settlement for the island.
